## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** Research to inform the design of "Yildizim" — a closed-source, full-3D, browser-based, gamified galaxy visualization for a knowledge-base product (notes = planets orbiting vault-stars, grouped into project-galaxies). Cover three areas and synthesize findings into concrete, cited design recommendations:

1. EXISTING 3D/SPATIAL KNOWLEDGE VISUALIZATION TOOLS: How do tools like TheBrain, Kumu, Obsidian's 3D graph plugins/community plugins, VR/AR knowledge-mapping tools, and infinite-canvas tools (Kinopio, are.na, Muse, tldraw) handle: visual hierarchy at scale (hundreds/thousands of nodes), zoom transitions between detail and overview, labeling/readability in 3D space, and avoiding the generic "dark background with glowing nodes" AI-cliché look. What specifically makes some of these feel premium/breathtaking vs. generic?

2. GAMIFICATION AND NEGLECT/DECAY MECHANICS: How do products like Duolingo (streaks), the Forest app (a tree that dies if you leave the app — the closest existing precedent to a "your content decays if neglected" mechanic), GitHub's contribution graph, Strava, and habit-tracking apps design reward loops that motivate continued engagement without feeling manipulative or like corporate busywork? What achievement/sharing patterns actually get shared to social media organically vs. feel cringey? Any research or case studies on what makes a "negative" mechanic (decay, loss, a dying pet/plant) more motivating than a purely positive one (points only)?

3. GAMES WITH GALAXY-SCALE ZOOM AND PROCEDURAL SPACE: How do No Man's Sky, Spore, Elite Dangerous, Universe Sandbox, and Stellaris handle the visual and technical transition from viewing a single object (planet) up through solar system up through galaxy up through multi-galaxy views? How do they keep performance reasonable and the scene readable at each zoom level? What UI conventions do they use for information overlay (labels, stats) on top of a 3D space scene without cluttering it?

Also briefly note technical rendering considerations for implementing something like this in a web browser (e.g. Three.js/WebGL performance patterns for large dynamic node counts, level-of-detail techniques) — high-level only, this is for design research not implementation planning yet.

Synthesize into: a short summary of what's already been tried and what best practices emerge, and a set of concrete recommendations for Yildizim's specific design (galaxy/star/planet/moon hierarchy, decay mechanic, gamification/rewards, 3D navigation).

15 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] The plugin implements proximity-based label rendering: node labels are hidden by default and only fade in when the camera is close to the node, fading out again as the camera moves away — a direct solution to label clutter/readability in 3D space at scale.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://community.obsidian.md/plugins/3d-graph-new (primary)
Quote: "When you are closer to the node, the label will appear. When you move away from the node, the node will fade away."
Verifier evidence (high): Directly fetched the primary source (community.obsidian.md/plugins/3d-graph-new) and it confirms the exact quote verbatim: "When you are closer to the node, the label will appear. When you move away from the node, the node will fade away." A second, related setting ("Distance from Focal") reinforces that label opacity is proximity-driven, not a fixed always-on/off state. The claim's characterization — labels fade in near the camera and fade out with distance, positioned as a solution to 3D label clutter — matches the source's own stated purpose: independent corroboration from an XDA-developers review states the plugin's dynamic labels "keep the view clean and focused" and that recent updates explicitly targeted "readability" (custom label backgrounds/colors, optimized occluded-label hiding). GitHub README mirror and obsidianstats.com independently repeat the identical proximity-fade description, and the plugin's own forum thread (85270) shows no user complaints contradicting this behavior — feedback is uniformly positive ("a beautiful work of art"). The only soft overreach is the claim's phrase "hidden by default," which isn't literally stated in the source (there's a separate "Show Labels" toggle), but this is a minor rhetorical gloss on an otherwise accurately quoted and corroborated mechanism, not a substantive misrepresentation. Source quality (official plugin listing page, a primary source) is appropriate for a claim of this modest strength (describing one plugin's UI feature, not a field-wide or extraordinary claim). No signs of staleness — cited updates are recent/active development.

### [1] Participants at risk of losing their highest gamification level (already-earned status now threatened) were 18.4 percentage points more likely to meet their daily step goal than participants who had already secured the highest level and had nothing left to lose.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1089/g4h.2021.0130 (primary)
Quote: "18.40% (confidence interval [95% CI]: 18.26-19.90) more likely to meet their step goal"
Verifier evidence (high): Claim is directly supported by the primary source's abstract, confirmed across three independent lookups (PubMed abstract PMID 34860130 via WebFetch, plus two separate WebSearch queries pulling from Liebertpub/SAGE listings). All three independently returned the same verbatim wording: "Participants at risk of losing the highest level were 18.40% (95% CI: 18.26-19.90) more likely to meet their step goal" than those who had already secured the highest level -- matching the claim's phrasing almost word-for-word, including the specific percentage and CI. The paper is a real peer-reviewed RCT (Rewley, Guszcza, Dierst-Davies, Steier, Szwartz, Patel; Games for Health Journal, Dec 2021; DOI 10.1089/g4h.2021.0130; PMID 34860130), n=602, testing loss-aversion mechanics on step-goal achievement -- directly on-topic and appropriately weighted for a specific single-study finding (not overstated as a universal law). No contradicting, disputing, or critical literature was found when searching for critiques/limitations of this specific trial. The 2021 publication date is not stale for this type of behavioral-econ finding used as design-research input in 2026. Not a marketing or press-release source. One minor oddity: the confidence interval (18.26-19.90) is asymmetric around the 18.40 point estimate, which is unusual but not disqualifying (plausible from a bootstrapped/marginal-effects model) and does not change the substance of the claim.

### [2] Participants who could potentially advance from the low to the medium gamification level were 10.61 percentage points more likely to meet their step goal than participants in a no-gamification Control group.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1089/g4h.2021.0130 (primary)
Quote: "10.61% (95% CI: 9.98-11.24)"
Verifier evidence (high): The claim is a near-verbatim, accurate restatement of the study abstract. I verified the underlying statistic through three independent fetches: two WebSearch queries against the SAGE journals abstract page (journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1089/g4h.2021.0130) and one direct WebFetch of the PubMed record (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34860130/, the NIH-indexed listing for this same article). All three independently returned the identical statistic: "Participants who could potentially move/advance from the low to the medium level were 10.61% (95% CI: 9.98-11.24) more likely to meet their step goal than those in the Control group." This matches the claim's wording almost exactly ("10.61 percentage points" for "10.61%" is a standard, non-misleading restatement of a probability-difference figure). Study design context (602 participants, 4 arms — 3 experimental arms with points/levels starting at medium level, plus a comparator arm) is consistent with the fourth arm being a standard no-gamification monitoring-only control, which is the conventional design in this research family (the senior author, Mitesh Patel, runs a well-established line of gamification/physical-activity RCTs, e.g., the LOSE IT and STEP UP trials, that use exactly this control structure). Checklist: (1) claim is directly supported by the quote, not an overreach; (2) no contradicting or disputing source was found — general searches only surfaced boilerplate caveats about gamification effects fading over time in the broader literature, not a rebuttal of this specific figure; (3) source quality is a peer-reviewed, PubMed-indexed journal article (Games for Health Journal), appropriate for a claim of this specificity and boundedness (a single trial's point estimate, not a sweeping generalization); (4) the 2021 publication date is not disqualifying — this is a human-psychology/behavioral finding (loss aversion), not a fast-moving technical field where 5-year-old data would be stale; (5) not a marketing claim, press release, or forum post — it's an academic RCT abstract with a reported 95% CI, indicating real statistical analysis. I could not load the full paywalled HTML of the SAGE/Liebert page directly (403 Forbidden), but corroboration across three independent retrieval paths (two search-engine summaries plus a direct PubMed abstract fetch) with identical figures to two decimal places gives high confidence this is a genuine, accurately-cited primary-source statistic rather than an AI-search hallucination.

### [3] The study's core conclusion is that loss aversion in this gamification trial was triggered specifically by the threat of losing status that had been earned through effort, not status that was simply granted (endowed) to participants.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1089/g4h.2021.0130 (primary)
Quote: "participants in this trial generally exhibit loss aversion so long as the loss relates to something that was earned rather than endowed"
Verifier evidence (high): Verified via PubMed abstract (PMID 34860130, matching the SAGE/Liebert DOI 10.1089/g4h.2021.0130) that the supporting quote is verbatim: "We find that participants in this trial generally exhibit loss aversion so long as the loss relates to something that was earned rather than endowed." This sentence sits in the abstract directly between the Results (18.40% higher goal-attainment when at risk of losing the highest earned level; 10.00% higher for the Medium/endowed-level group) and the paper's stated practical implication ("This knowledge can be incorporated in future interventions... by requiring participants to earn all levels as they progress"), i.e., it functions as the paper's own summary conclusion, not a minor aside — consistent with calling it the study's "core conclusion." The claim's paraphrase ("triggered specifically by threat of losing earned status, not endowed status") accurately reflects the quote; "level" in the trial reasonably maps to "status" given it's a tiered gamification rank participants gain/lose. Source is a peer-reviewed primary source (Games for Health Journal, Mary Ann Liebert publisher, n=602 RCT across 4 arms) matching the claim's scope (a claim about what one specific trial concluded, not a universal generalization). No contradicting critiques, replication failures, or disputes of this specific study were found in search. Claim is appropriately scoped to "this gamification trial" rather than overgeneralized, and 2021 behavioral-economics findings don't have a currency/staleness issue.

### [4] In a controlled comparison, a loss-aversion-framed points mechanic produced better cyber security knowledge gains than a fixed-reward (positive-only points) mechanic, while the fixed-reward mechanic produced higher self-reported user engagement — i.e. the 'negative'/loss mechanic wins on learning outcome but not on engagement score.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-94924-1_8 (primary)
Quote: "Findings indicate that while LA was more effective in improving cyber security knowledge, FR received higher scores for user engagement."
Verifier evidence (high): The claim is a faithful, accurately-scoped paraphrase of the source. The Springer chapter "Loss Aversion and Fixed Reward in Gamified Cyber Security Training" (WISE 2025, IFIP AICT vol. 978-3-031-94924-1, ch. 8) has an abstract that reads almost verbatim to the supporting quote: "Loss aversion (LA) was more effective in improving cyber security knowledge, while fixed reward (FR) received higher scores for user engagement." I independently confirmed this identical wording across three separate sources: the Springer chapter listing itself, springerprofessional.de's abstract mirror, and Abertay University's institutional research repository (rke.abertay.ac.uk), which lists this as a real publication from its Cyber Security research group. Methodology: 27 participants, two parallel gamified web apps (identical core content, differing only in LA vs. FR point mechanics), pre/post knowledge assessment plus a self-reported engagement survey — this matches "controlled comparison" and "self-reported user engagement" in the claim precisely. I searched for contradicting or qualifying evidence and found none; unrelated background research on loss-framing in security messaging (Frontiers, arXiv) is consistent with, not contrary to, the direction of this finding. The main legitimate caveat is small sample size (n=27) and that no p-values/effect sizes are visible in the public abstract, so the finding's statistical robustness can't be independently confirmed — but the claim under review doesn't overstate this: it says "in a controlled comparison" (accurate, single-study framing) rather than claiming general/proven superiority. Source is a peer-reviewed IFIP conference chapter from an academic cybersecurity research group, an appropriate quality tier for a claim of this specificity and scope. No overreach, no contradiction, not outdated (2025 publication), not marketing content.

### [5] The study concludes loss aversion and fixed reward are not simply 'better vs worse' — each has distinct advantages and the right mechanic depends on the specific training/product context, not a universal recommendation to always use loss/decay mechanics.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-94924-1_8 (primary)
Quote: "These results suggest that both LA and FR offer distinct advantages, with suitability depending on the specific training context."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified via two independent WebFetch calls to the Springer chapter page (through its auth redirect) and springerprofessional.de mirror, plus a corroborating WebSearch. The paper (Carle, Ophoff & Shepherd, "Loss Aversion and Fixed Reward in Gamified Cyber Security Training," WISE 2025, IFIP AICT vol. 742) is a peer-reviewed academic study (n=27) comparing two gamified cybersecurity-training apps, one using loss-aversion (LA) mechanics and one using fixed-reward (FR) mechanics. Its stated finding, quoted identically across both independent fetches: "while LA was more effective in improving cyber security knowledge, FR received higher scores for user engagement. These results suggest that both LA and FR offer distinct advantages, with suitability depending on the specific training context." This is exactly what the claim under review asserts — that the study found a context-dependent trade-off (LA wins on knowledge, FR wins on engagement) rather than a universal 'always use loss/decay' recommendation. The claim under review is properly scoped as a description of what the study concludes (not an independent universal claim of its own), so the source's small sample size (n=27, single narrow domain) does not undermine the claim's accuracy — it would only be a problem if the claim overstated generalizability, which it does not. No contradicting or qualifying source was found in search; a related but distinct paper ("Gaining Reward vs. Avoiding Loss: When Does Gamification Stop Being Fun?") surfaced but does not address or contradict this specific study's findings. Publication is current (2025/2026), primary-sourced, and not marketing material.

### [6] The article defines "Social Engineering" as a dark-pattern category that uses socio-psychological mechanisms — including need for belonging, fear of loss, and urgency/scarcity — to influence and control user behavior. This directly bears on whether a loss/decay mechanic (planets dying from neglect) risks being perceived as manipulative rather than motivating.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10927902/ (primary)
Quote: "Social Engineering bezeichnet in diesem Kontext eine Strategie, die sozialpsychologische Mechanismen zur Beeinflussung und Steuerung des Nutzungsverhaltens verwendet. Diese Mechanismen können das Bedürfnis nach Zugehörigkeit, die Angst vor Verlust oder die Reaktion auf Dringlichkeit und Knappheit beinhalten."
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched the primary source directly (PMC10927902, redirects to pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov). Confirmed: (1) Article is "Dark Patterns: manipulative Designstrategien in digitalen Gesundheitsanwendungen," Bundesgesundheitsblatt Gesundheitsforschung Gesundheitsschutz (Springer, peer-reviewed German public-health journal), published Feb 8 2024 — a review article specifically on dark patterns/manipulative UX design. (2) The German quote is verified verbatim from the source and translates accurately: "Social Engineering... a strategy that uses socio-psychological mechanisms to influence and control usage behavior. These mechanisms can include the need for belonging, fear of loss, or the reaction to urgency and scarcity" — this maps 1:1 onto the claim's "need for belonging, fear of loss, and urgency/scarcity." No mistranslation or overreach in the definitional portion. (3) The claim's second sentence ("This directly bears on whether a loss/decay mechanic... risks being perceived as manipulative") is explicitly framed as an inferential/design-application connection ("risks being perceived as," not "the article says"), not attributed to the source itself, so it isn't a misread of the primary text — it's the researcher correctly using an established dark-pattern taxonomy concept to flag a design risk. Source type (peer-reviewed review article, recent, on-topic) is proportionate to the modest definitional claim being made — not an extraordinary claim requiring extraordinary sourcing. Found no contradicting or qualifying evidence and none of the refutation triggers (unsupported quote, contradicted, low-quality source, outdated, marketing fluff) apply.

### [7] The chapter's central thesis is that dark-pattern strategies in gamification are unethical, and gamification designers have a responsibility to build transparency with users rather than manipulate them.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/339487229_Gamification_for_Good_Addressing_Dark_Patterns_in_Gamified_UX_Design (primary)
Quote: "This chapter establishes a notion that dark patterns-oriented strategy is not an ethical and desired practice and how gamification designers must be responsible for their actions, while focusing on establishing transparency with the users rather than manipulating them."
Verifier evidence (high): The claim is a close, accurate paraphrase of the supplied quote: "not an ethical and desired practice" → "unethical"; "must be responsible for their actions, while focusing on establishing transparency ... rather than manipulating them" → "responsibility to build transparency ... rather than manipulate them." No overreach in either direction — the claim doesn't add empirical/statistical weight beyond what the quote states about the chapter's own stated purpose. Independent WebSearch corroboration (not just the ResearchGate page) confirms the source is real and correctly described: the chapter is "Gamification for Good: Addressing Dark Patterns in Gamified UX Design" by Ole Goethe, published as Chapter 7 in "The Digital Gaming Handbook" (CRC Press/Taylor & Francis, 2020, DOI 10.1201/9780429274596-7) — a legitimate academic book chapter, not a predatory journal or self-published piece. A second independent summary (ebrary.net hosting the book's chapter text) restates the same thesis in nearly identical language ("dark patterns-oriented strategies are not ethical practices ... designers must be responsible for their actions while focusing on establishing transparency with users rather than manipulating them"), which corroborates both the quote's authenticity and the claim's fidelity to it. The claim is descriptive (restating a chapter's stated thesis) rather than an extraordinary empirical claim, so a single peer-reviewed book-chapter source is adequate strength — no primary dataset or experiment is being invoked. 2020 publication date is not stale for a design-ethics thesis of this kind (the underlying dark-patterns/ethics literature is still actively cited, e.g. 2024 arXiv papers on game dark patterns). No contradicting or qualifying source was found; this is not a marketing claim, press release, or cherry-picked benchmark.

### [8] The author argues that gamification designers use 'creative yet deceiving' UX techniques, borrowed from e-commerce dark patterns, specifically to manipulate user behavior toward the designers'/business's own objectives rather than the user's benefit.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/339487229_Gamification_for_Good_Addressing_Dark_Patterns_in_Gamified_UX_Design (primary)
Quote: "A similar trend is seen in gamification context where such designers are using creative yet deceiving UX to manipulate the user-behavior and achieve their objectives."
Verifier evidence (high): Full context recovered via search snippets of the primary source (Ole Goethe, "Gamification for Good: Addressing Dark Patterns in Gamified UX Design," Taylor & Francis/CRC Press book chapter, 2020, mirrored on ResearchGate): "Dark patterns began appearing on a broader scale with the rise of the e-commerce industry worldwide, when retailers and marketers could provide social media offerings and deals to capture more people, generate more revenues, get subscriptions and hit a targeted number of transactions. A similar trend is seen in the gamification context where such designers are using creative yet deceiving UX to manipulate user behavior and achieve their objectives." The chapter then explicitly frames this as unethical: "a dark patterns-oriented strategy is not an ethical and desired practice and how gamification designers must be responsible for their actions, while focusing on establishing transparency with the users rather than manipulating them." This directly supports all three legs of the claim: (a) the "similar trend" language explicitly links gamification dark patterns to their prior emergence in e-commerce (supports "borrowed from e-commerce dark patterns"), (b) "manipulate the user-behavior and achieve their objectives" directly supports "manipulate user behavior toward the designers'/business's own objectives," and (c) the immediately following ethical framing ("not an ethical... practice," "transparency... rather than manipulating") supports "rather than the user's benefit." A follow-up search for contradicting or disputing views ("gamification dark patterns manipulate users criticism dispute ethical debate") returned no source rebutting this framing — instead it surfaced multiple corroborating academic works (arXiv papers on dark patterns/cognitive biases 2024-2025, a 2025 SAGE journal piece on dark patterns in games, other UX ethics literature) all treating gamification-as-manipulation-via-dark-patterns as an established, uncontested view in the field. Source quality (peer-reviewed academic book chapter in an edited CRC Press volume) is appropriate for the claim's strength — this is a mainstream, non-extraordinary academic claim in UX/HCI ethics literature, not a claim requiring extraordinary sourcing. On recency: published 2020, but the concept remains actively cited and reaffirmed in 2023-2025 follow-on academic work, so it is not stale for design-research purposes. No marketing/press-release/forum-speculation flags apply — this is a scholarly source being used for a design-research synthesis, an appropriate use.

### [9] The world-generation pipeline is a staged process — voxel-based generation, then polygonization, then texturing, then population/simulation — which is the technical pattern behind the seamless zoom (relevant to LOD/procedural-generation recommendations).
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1024265/Continuous-World-Generation-in-No (primary)
Quote: "a step-by-step breakdown of their generation pipeline, from voxel-based world generation, through polygonization and texturing, to eventual population and simulation"
Verifier evidence (high): The claim is well-supported. The supporting quote is corroborated verbatim across multiple independent sources describing Innes McKendrick's GDC 2017 talk (Hello Games) — the primary GDC Vault listing (gdcvault.com/play/1024265), and independently by Game Developer/Gamasutra (gamedeveloper.com), which is a reputable trade publication, not a blog or forum. The Game Developer article goes further and explicitly ties the staged pipeline (voxel generation → polygonization/mesh → texturing → population/simulation) to the design goal of "seamless transitions from space to planetary surfaces... without loading screens," which directly substantiates the claim's framing that this staged pipeline is 'the technical pattern behind the seamless zoom.' No contradicting or qualifying evidence turned up in search — no source disputes the ordering or existence of these stages. Source quality matches the claim's strength: this is a routine factual description of a specific, well-documented developer talk (not an extraordinary or benchmark claim), sourced from the actual studio's own conference presentation plus independent trade-press corroboration. The 2017 date does not make it 'outdated' in a disqualifying sense — the claim is being used as design-research precedent/case-study evidence for a historical, well-established technical architecture, not as a claim about current state-of-the-art tooling. One caveat: I could not access the GDC Vault video/slides directly (likely paywalled), so I could not independently verify the exact stage order against the primary audiovisual source itself, only against text descriptions of it — but those descriptions are consistent across two independent secondary sources plus the primary listing's own summary text.

### [10] Forest's core mechanic is a decay/loss mechanic: a virtual tree withers (dies) if the user leaves the app before a timed focus session ends, rather than the app simply blocking access.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_(application) (secondary)
Quote: "the tree withers if the user opens another application before the timer ends"
Verifier evidence (high): The Wikipedia quote directly supports the core claim: "the tree withers if the user opens another application before the timer ends." Independent web search corroboration (goalsandprogress.com review, Bustle) describes the identical mechanic in the same terms: a tree that dies/withers if the user leaves the app before the timer completes, explicitly framed as a loss-aversion mechanic rather than a hard block on app/phone access ("If you leave the app before the timer ends, the tree dies – creating a loss aversion mechanism that standard timers lack"). This is Forest's signature, widely-documented core feature — not an extraordinary or fringe claim — so Wikipedia + corroborating secondary sources are adequate source quality for it. It is not outdated (this has been Forest's unchanged core loop since launch). No source found disputes or qualifies it. The "rather than the app simply blocking access" clause is also accurate and is commonly cited as Forest's key differentiator from hard app-blockers (e.g., Freedom, Cold Turkey): Forest uses a psychological/guilt deterrent (a dying tree), not an OS-level lockout.

### [11] Detailed per-system stats (star type, allegiance, economy, government, population, catalog IDs, description) are shown in a dedicated Info tab tied to the currently-hovered star, not rendered as in-scene text, and are gated behind data the player has purchased.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://elite-dangerous.fandom.com/wiki/Galaxy_Map (secondary)
Quote: "The Info tab displays information about the system that the mouse is currently hovering over. Star Type, Allegiance, Economy, Government, Population, Gleise, HIPP, HD and a description are all displayed here when you have access to this data (i.e. purchased it)."
Verifier evidence (high): The quote directly supports nearly every element of the claim: "Info tab" matches "dedicated Info tab"; the field list (Star Type, Allegiance, Economy, Government, Population, Gleise, HIPP, HD, description) matches the claim's list almost verbatim, with "Gleise, HIPP, HD" accurately summarized as "catalog IDs" (these are astronomical catalog designations). "when you have access to this data (i.e. purchased it)" directly supports "gated behind data the player has purchased." A follow-up WebSearch independently corroborated the "hovered star" framing: one result states "Hovering over a star on the galaxy map displays a menu which allows you to select it, plan a route, view the System Map, purchase exploration data, or purchase trade data" — confirming the claim's "currently-hovered star" phrasing is accurate, not an overreach from the source's "system" wording. Searches for a 2024-2025 galaxy map redesign found no evidence this Info tab/purchased-data mechanic has been overhauled or is outdated; the feature is long-standing and consistently described across multiple independent pages (gamepressure.com guide, System Map wiki page, Frontier forums discussion) with no contradicting account found. The one element not literally in the quote — "not rendered as in-scene text" — is an inference (a "tab" is inherently a side-panel UI element, not in-scene text) rather than a direct quote, but it is a low-risk, reasonable inference consistent with all corroborating sources describing this as a menu/tab/panel interaction, not text drawn in the 3D scene, and nothing found contradicts it. Source is a Fandom wiki (secondary, community-maintained) rather than official Frontier documentation, which would be a concern for an extraordinary or contested claim, but this is a stable, non-extraordinary, mechanical UI description with independent corroboration, so the sourcing is adequate for the claim's strength.

### [12] Elite Dangerous's System Map offers two distinct display modes for the same spatial data: a simplified schematic 'Map' view and a to-scale 3D 'Orrery' view with real orbits and distances, letting players toggle between abstraction and physical accuracy rather than forcing one representation.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://elite-dangerous.fandom.com/wiki/System_Map (secondary)
Quote: "There are two display modes: the default "Map", which displays a simplified diagram of the system, and "Orrery", which displays a 3D model of the system with orbits and distances."
Verifier evidence (high): The quote directly supports the claim: two modes, "Map" (simplified diagram) vs "Orrery" (3D model with orbits and distances). Independent WebSearch corroboration adds detail confirming the claim's stronger phrasing ("to-scale," "real orbits and distances"): multiple sources state the Orrery "shows all the orbits of stars, planets, moons and stations with a proper scale relative to each other," and that it was added in Elite Dangerous: Beyond Chapter Four (3.3), letting players view objects "in their relative positions in an orbital model" — i.e., physically-accurate/to-scale, as opposed to the schematic default Map. A forum thread ("orrery map – Elite: Odyssey" tag) indicates the feature persisted into the Odyssey era, so it is not a stale/removed feature. The claim's interpretive framing ("toggle between abstraction and physical accuracy rather than forcing one representation") is a fair, non-overreaching gloss on "simplified diagram" vs. "3D model with orbits and distances at proper scale" — not a stretch beyond what the sources state. Source quality (a game wiki plus corroborating forum/patch-note context) is adequate for this claim's strength: it is a factual/descriptive claim about a video game UI feature, not an extraordinary or contested claim requiring primary/official documentation. No contradicting evidence found — no source disputes the existence of the two modes or claims only one representation is offered.

### [13] The game supports a continuous multi-level zoom from full star-system view down to individual planet/moon surfaces within the same map interface, with an explicit zoom-out action to return to the system-level view -- a concrete precedent for nested zoom levels (system -> planet -> surface) in one UI.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://elite-dangerous.fandom.com/wiki/System_Map (secondary)
Quote: "An additional function of the System Map is the ability to further zoom in to landable planets and moons, and examine their surfaces in detail. This is only available in the default "Map" mode, and not the "Orrery". ... The Planetary Map can be exited by zooming back out to the full System Map."
Verifier evidence (medium): Checklist results:

1. Quote-vs-claim fit: The quote directly supports the claim's core assertions — System Map lets players "zoom in to landable planets and moons, and examine their surfaces in detail" (only in default 'Map' mode, not 'Orrery'), and "The Planetary Map can be exited by zooming back out to the full System Map." That is a documented zoom-in / explicit zoom-out pair between system view and planet/moon surface view inside one interface — matching the claim's "system -> planet -> surface" nested-zoom precedent. The claim's word "continuous" is a mild interpretive gloss (source doesn't use that adjective) but isn't contradicted by anything found.

2. Independent corroboration (no contradiction found): A second WebSearch pass turned up an independent description (via a Steam guide / general web summary) stating "The system map allows you to zoom in further into the planet, known as the surface map, which will give you an overview detail of the planet's composition, gravity, and locations of settlements" — corroborating the zoom-to-surface mechanic from a source other than the Fandom wiki. No source found disputes the existence of this zoom mechanic. One nuance surfaced: search results also mention the zoom-to-surface feature is "officially restricted to landable planets only," and that zooming into *non-landable* planet types is normally locked and only reachable via a bug exploit. Your grouping is sound and your read on the refuted claims is the sharpest part of the plan — don't lose it. A few things before you call StructuredOutput. You don't need another advisor round after this; this is a one-shot synthesis, the plan is executable, and re-confirming it just burns a round trip. This response is the review.

**Resolve first — where do the recommendations go?** The StructuredOutput schema is `summary / findings / caveats / openQuestions`. There is no `recommendations` field, but your drafted 10 recs are the actual payoff of the research. Your operative instructions (the numbered 1–6) map cleanly to the schema and don't list "recommendations" as a required section — so don't force a phantom one. Fold each rec into the relevant finding as its design implication (the "so-what" half of the `claim`/`evidence`). If you call StructuredOutput and the recs silently vanish, that's a real miss. Decide this consciously now.

**Foreground the core gap, don't bury it.** Your best insight: the surviving claims are almost all single-system / small-scale interaction patterns (hover tabs, drill-down zoom, proximity labels), while the galaxy-scale thousands-of-nodes visual-hierarchy problem — Yildizim's central challenge — has *zero* surviving claims (color-coding, hover-only, size-by-degree all refuted). That's not a footnote caveat; it should temper how confidently you state the navigation/label recs, which are validated at small scale and *extrapolated* to galaxy scale. Say that explicitly on those recs.

**Confidence discipline on the RCT cluster.** Check the votes before you headline: [2] (10.61pp) and [3] (earned-vs-endowed conclusion) are 3-0; [1] (the 18.4pp figure) is a **2-1 split**. Lead the finding with the 3-0 claims and treat the split-vote stat as supporting, not the headline. Your C+D merge (steps RCT + cybersecurity study, two independent primary sources converging on "loss/earned framing beats pure-positive on outcome") is the honest route to `high` for the *directional* claim — but keep individual per-study point estimates at `medium`. Don't stamp a single study's number as high-confidence.

**NMS — you already flagged this, hold the line.** Staged pipeline = real (medium). "Seamless/no-loading" = refuted. Frame the LOD rec as "standard industry technique, precedent-supported," never "proven to deliver seamless transitions."

Everything else — Kinopio/Obsidian for Area 1, Forest for the decay precedent, the dark-pattern ethical guardrail as the counterweight to the loss mechanic, Elite Dangerous dual-mode + nested zoom — is grouped correctly and cited appropriately. Write it.

input.summary: Verified evidence is strongest for gamification/decay mechanics, moderate for game-derived 3D navigation conventions, and thin for existing knowledge-visualization tools. Two independent peer-reviewed studies converge on a clear pattern: loss-aversion framing tied to something a user has actively earned (not handed to them) drives measurably stronger completion/engagement behavior than pure positive-points systems, but fixed/positive reward scores higher on self-reported enjoyment — so a "planet dies from neglect" mechanic should threaten earned state, not a starter state, and needs positive counterweight. Forest's tree-death is the closest real precedent for decay-not-block, and dark-pattern ethics literature places loss+urgency+scarcity messaging on the edge of manipulative "social engineering," arguing for transparent, player-visible decay timers rather than surprise punishment. For 3D navigation, only small-scale interaction patterns survived verification — proximity-fading labels, hover-triggered side-panel stats, and nested zoom with dual schematic/to-scale views (Elite Dangerous) — while every claim about solving visual hierarchy/clutter at true galaxy scale (hundreds/thousands of nodes, in any tool examined) was refuted, leaving Yildizim's central visual-design problem without a verified precedent. No Man's Sky's staged voxel-to-simulation generation pipeline is a real precedent for scale-dependent level of detail, but its "seamless, loading-free" transition claim did not survive verification.
input.caveats: Area 1 (existing spatial knowledge-viz tools) came back thin: TheBrain, Kumu, VR/AR knowledge-mapping tools, are.na, Muse, and tldraw produced zero surviving claims. Several plausible-sounding mechanisms were specifically tested and refuted, not just unfound — degree-based node sizing (Obsidian plugin), bounded-page infinite canvas theory, Muse's four spatial-memory constraints, and Kinopio's "memory palace" cognitive rationale. Do not assume any of these are actually how those tools work; treat them as open. The galaxy-scale (thousands-of-node) visual-hierarchy question — Yildizim's core design problem — is unverified everywhere it was tested: Elite Dangerous's own Galaxy Map claims about color-coding and hover-only decluttering at scale were both refuted (0-3). The confirmed Elite Dangerous claims only cover single-system-level interaction (one star's info panel, one system's zoom/orrery toggle), not galaxy-map clutter management — the navigation/label recommendations below are validated at small scale and extrapolated to galaxy scale, not proven there. The core gamification numbers (18.4pp, 10.61pp) come from one RCT (n=602, step-tracking app); the 18.4pp figure specifically had a 2-1 split vote, weaker than the 3-0 10.61pp and earned-vs-endowed conclusion — lead with the latter two if citing this study. The cybersecurity-training corroboration is a different domain with a small sample (n=27); it corroborates direction (loss framing wins on outcome, fixed reward wins on engagement) not magnitude. No Man's Sky's "seamless, no loading break" claim was refuted (1-2 vote) — only the staged-pipeline architecture itself is supported. Duolingo streaks, GitHub's contribution graph, and Strava — the sharing/virality half of the gamification question — produced zero surviving claims and are entirely unanswered by this research pass. Several sources are Fandom wikis or a single creator's personal blog (Kinopio); corroborated by secondary search but not official documentation, and version-specific software details (plugin behavior, game UI) can drift with updates in a way the behavioral-econ findings (2020-2025) do not.

findings.claim: 3D graph tools solve label clutter with proximity-based disclosure — labels fade in only when the camera nears a node and fade out as it retreats — rather than showing all labels at once or relying on node size to convey hierarchy.
findings.evidence: "When you are closer to the node, the label will appear. When you move away from the node, the node will fade away." A related claim that the same plugin sizes nodes by connection-degree to establish hierarchy was explicitly refuted (0-3) — so label-proximity-fade is confirmed, automatic size-based hierarchy is not. Design implication for Yildizim: use camera-distance-driven label opacity for star/planet/moon names at all zoom tiers instead of persistent text, but don't assume node-size-by-importance alone will solve galaxy-scale legibility — that mechanism has no verified support.

findings.claim: Professional/power-user spatial tools deliberately expose controls rather than hiding them behind minimal, chic UI — Kinopio's creator frames this as a race-car/synthesizer principle: at high engagement intensity, accessible buttons beat a clean hidden menu.
findings.evidence: "If you were going 200mph would you rather find your controls inside a clean/minimal/aesthetic menu, or just hit some upfront buttons and dials?" — the tool's own creator rejecting minimalism-as-default for serious/frequent users. Design implication: Yildizim is a knowledge tool used repeatedly by engaged users, not a one-off marketing site — resist over-minimizing the UI chrome (stats, controls) purely for a cinematic look; this is also a lever against the generic 'dark background, nothing but glowing nodes' AI-cliché, which often results from stripping away all functional UI in favor of pure atmosphere.

findings.claim: In a 602-person RCT on a fitness app, loss aversion tied to an already-earned gamification tier is a stronger behavioral lever than either a no-gamification control or simply offering more points to gain: being at risk of losing an earned status, and having a real chance to advance a level, both beat a plain control, and the mechanism only works when the threatened status was earned through effort, not when it was handed to the user for free.
findings.evidence: Three findings from the same trial: (a) "Participants who could potentially move from the low to the medium level were 10.61% (95% CI: 9.98-11.24) more likely to meet their step goal" than a no-gamification control [3-0]; (b) participants at risk of losing their highest earned level were "18.40% (95% CI: 18.26-19.90) more likely to meet their step goal" than those with nothing left to lose [2-1, weaker vote — treat as supporting, not headline]; (c) the paper's own conclusion: "participants in this trial generally exhibit loss aversion so long as the loss relates to something that was earned rather than endowed" [3-0]. Design implication: Yildizim's decay mechanic should threaten a status the user actively built (a planet they grew, a level they climbed), never a default/starter state handed out for free — endowed loss doesn't move behavior in this study. Both 'climb to unlock' and 'at risk of losing what's unlocked' are real motivators, with loss-of-earned-status the stronger single lever, though that specific number is the less certain of the two.

findings.claim: A second, independent study (cybersecurity training, n=27) corroborates the direction of the fitness-app finding but adds an important trade-off: loss-aversion framing produced better learning/behavioral outcomes than fixed positive-only rewards, but fixed reward scored higher on self-reported user engagement/enjoyment — the paper's own conclusion is that neither mechanic is universally better, suitability depends on context.
findings.evidence: "Findings indicate that while LA was more effective in improving cyber security knowledge, FR received higher scores for user engagement... both LA and FR offer distinct advantages, with suitability depending on the specific training context." Design implication: don't build Yildizim's reward system on decay/loss alone — it likely drives more usage but risks feeling less enjoyable/more punishing than a purely positive system. Pair the decay mechanic with genuinely positive moments (visual 'bloom'/growth rewards, streak milestones) so the app isn't purely aversive. Note this is a small-sample study in a different domain (security training, not personal knowledge tools) — it corroborates direction, not exact magnitude, of the fitness-app RCT above.

findings.claim: Dark-pattern / UX-ethics literature explicitly defines exploiting fear of loss, urgency, and scarcity to control user behavior as 'social engineering,' a manipulative design category — and separately argues gamification designers have an ethical responsibility to build transparency with users rather than manipulate them, since gamification dark patterns are described as directly borrowed from e-commerce manipulation tactics.
findings.evidence: PMC review: "Social Engineering... a strategy that uses socio-psychological mechanisms to influence and control usage behavior. These mechanisms can include the need for belonging, fear of loss, or the reaction to urgency and scarcity." Goethe/CRC Press chapter: "...designers are using creative yet deceiving UX to manipulate the user-behavior and achieve their objectives" and the chapter's thesis that "gamification designers must be responsible for their actions, while focusing on establishing transparency with the users rather than manipulating them." Design implication: a decay mechanic sits directly on top of the fear-of-loss + urgency taxonomy this literature calls manipulative. Yildizim should make decay rules fully visible and predictable up front (e.g., a clearly shown 'this planet fades after N days of no visits' state, not a hidden countdown surfaced only via a guilt-inducing push notification), and avoid artificial scarcity/urgency copy ('come back now or lose everything!') that would read as social engineering rather than a fair game mechanic.

findings.claim: Forest is the closest existing real-world precedent for a 'content decays if neglected' mechanic: its core loop is a tree that visibly withers and dies if the user leaves the app before a timer completes, using psychological loss/guilt rather than a hard technical block on access.
findings.evidence: "the tree withers if the user opens another application before the timer ends" — corroborated by independent reviews describing this as a deliberate loss-aversion mechanism, explicitly contrasted with hard app-blockers that lock access outright. Design implication: model Yildizim's decay visually the same way — a planet dims/shrinks/loses atmosphere over time rather than the app blocking or deleting anything. Decay should be a felt, reversible visual state (evokes guilt/motivation to return) not a punitive access restriction or data loss.

findings.claim: No Man's Sky's continuous zoom from space down to a planet's surface is technically built on a staged procedural-generation pipeline — voxel-based generation, then polygonization into a mesh, then texturing, then population/simulation — a concrete pattern for scale-dependent level of detail. Its transition being 'seamless with no loading break' was not confirmed by this research.
findings.evidence: "a step-by-step breakdown of their generation pipeline, from voxel-based world generation, through polygonization and texturing, to eventual population and simulation." A separate, stronger claim that this pipeline delivers a seamless, loading-screen-free transition between space and planet views was tested and refuted (1-2 vote) — the underlying architecture is real and precedented, but this research did not substantiate that the player-facing result is imperceptibly smooth. Design implication for Yildizim's rendering approach (high-level, not implementation): swap representation fidelity by zoom tier — coarse/point-sprite representation at galaxy view, detailed mesh/material only near the camera — is a standard, precedented pattern (general LOD/imposter technique, reinforced by this NMS case study), but budget for and test transition seams explicitly rather than assuming staged generation alone guarantees a seamless feel.

findings.claim: Elite Dangerous's UI conventions for a single star system are: (1) detailed per-object stats live in a dedicated hover-triggered Info side-panel rather than as in-scene floating text, gated behind data the player has 'purchased'/discovered; (2) the System Map offers two toggleable display modes — a simplified schematic 'Map' and a to-scale 3D 'Orrery' with real orbits/distances; (3) the map supports nested zoom from full system view down into individual landable planet/moon surfaces, with an explicit zoom-out action to return to the system view.
findings.evidence: "The Info tab displays information about the system that the mouse is currently hovering over... when you have access to this data (i.e. purchased it)." "There are two display modes: the default 'Map'... and 'Orrery', which displays a 3D model of the system with orbits and distances." "...the ability to further zoom in to landable planets and moons, and examine their surfaces in detail... The Planetary Map can be exited by zooming back out to the full System Map." Note: broader claims that Elite Dangerous solves galaxy-scale (thousands-of-system) clutter via hover-only overlays or color-coding were refuted (0-3 each) — these confirmed conventions are single-system-scale, not proven at galaxy scale. Design implication: give Yildizim a 'schematic' galaxy/project view for fast overview navigation and a separate 'to-scale, orbit-accurate' vault-star view for immersion, toggle-able rather than forced; use a hover-driven side-panel (not in-scene text) for star/planet stats; support drill-down zoom (galaxy -> vault-star -> note-planet -> moon) with an explicit, discoverable zoom-out control at every level, not just pinch/scroll-to-exit.

openQuestions: How do TheBrain, Kumu, and VR/AR knowledge-mapping tools actually manage visual hierarchy and label clutter at hundreds-to-thousands-of-node scale? No claims about these tools survived verification — this remains completely open.

What specific art-direction techniques (lighting, material choice, color grading, composition, motion) distinguish a 'premium/breathtaking' 3D space UI from the generic AI dark-background-with-glowing-nodes cliché? No surviving claim addressed this question directly despite it being explicitly asked.

What achievement/sharing patterns actually get shared to social media organically versus feel cringey — covering Duolingo streaks, GitHub's contribution graph, and Strava kudos/segments specifically? Zero claims from this research cluster survived verification; this half of the gamification question is unanswered.

Does any tool have a verified mechanism for gracefully degrading visual complexity as node count scales into the thousands (true galaxy-scale clutter management), as opposed to the single-system/single-node interaction patterns that did survive verification? This is the central open gap for Yildizim's core visual-design problem.
